 Two Social Security Checks Will Become One. Which One the Survivor Will Keep, and What Will Disappear
 By Jake FitzGerald 
 Published November 13, 2026, 4:53am ET · 4 min read 
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 A widow keeps only the larger of her own check or her late husband's benefit, and the smaller one stops rather than being added together.
 Survivor payments start at about 72% of the late spouse's benefit and reach 100% at full retirement age, while his early claiming can cap her check.
 Filing single lowers the tax thresholds, so about 82% of the widow's benefits become taxable versus 49% before, though Medicare premiums stay standard.

 When one spouse dies, the household stops getting two Social Security retirement checks and keeps one. If a survivor qualifies for a survivor benefit and another benefit, the Social Security Administration says the payments “won’t be added together.” She gets the larger one. Rules already on file decide which check that is and how much it pays, and both answers change her taxes and her Medicare costs right away.
 How Social Security Picks the Check That Continues
 The survivor is paid the higher of two amounts: her own retirement benefit or the survivor benefit based on her late husband’s work record. In most couples the higher earner had the larger check, so the survivor benefit usually takes over and her own lower check stops. SSA lets a survivor switch benefits later. For example, she could start on survivor benefits and move to her own retirement benefit at age 70 if that payment is higher. This only helps a survivor who has not yet claimed her own benefit.
 Two Rules That Can Shrink the Survivor Check
 Her claiming age. SSA says survivor payments start at 71.5% of the late spouse’s benefit and rise to as much as 100% at the survivor’s full retirement age, which falls between ages 66 and 67.
 His claiming age. If the husband took a reduced retirement benefit early, SSA’s operations manual caps the widow’s benefit. She gets the larger of 82 1/2% of his primary insurance amount or the reduced benefit he would have been getting if he were still alive.
 A widow in her early 70s is past full retirement age, so the first rule no longer applies to her. The second rule depends on when her husband filed, which was decided years ago. (Survivor benefits run on their own schedule, separate from a retiree’s own benefit, and we walked through how couples should time the two decisions before 70 in a free guide here .)
 One Example, Before and After
 This hypothetical widow is 72. Her husband claimed at full retirement age, so neither reduction applies. After the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027, his check was $2,005 a month and hers was $1,350. Together that is $3,355, which matches SSA’s estimated 2027 average for an senior couple who both collect benefits. The $2,005 matches SSA’s estimated average for an senior widow(er) living alone.
 The couple took $40,000 a year in taxable IRA withdrawals, and she keeps withdrawing the same amount. She has no tax-exempt interest and no dependent child, so she files as single. The Social Security tax test uses the base amounts in IRS Publication 17 for tax year 2025. Medicare premiums use the 2026 CMS figures.

 What Disappears When the Smaller Check Stops
 Her own $1,350 check stops, which cuts household Social Security income by $16,200 a year. The taxable part of her benefits goes up slightly anyway. Publication 17’s worksheet gives single filers a $25,000 base amount and then a $9,000 band taxed at the lower rate. Joint filers get $32,000 and $12,000. Because the IRA withdrawals stay the same and the single thresholds are lower, more of each benefit dollar is taxed. In her case that is close to the federal limit of 85% of benefits under 26 U.S.C. § 86(a)(2)(B). On her return, that limit is $20,451.
 Where Her Medicare Premium Lands
 Under the 2026 CMS table, a single filer pays the standard Part B premium of $202.90 if her modified adjusted gross income is $109,000 or less. Her estimated income is $49,174.50 below that line. If her income goes over it, the first surcharge tier raises Part B to $284.10 a month and adds $14.50 a month to Part D. The household had been paying two premiums. Now it pays one.
 A large IRA withdrawal or a home sale reported on a single return could push her over the line. If a surcharge notice is based on a year when both spouses’ income counted, SSA lists the death of a spouse as a life-changing event. She can ask for a lower amount on Form SSA-44 .
 Social Security Paperwork That Confirms the Numbers
 Start with the notice SSA sends after the switch to survivor benefits. Check that the monthly amount matches the larger of the two benefits. If the husband claimed early, also check that the 82 1/2% floor was applied. Next January, use the total in box 5 of Form SSA-1099. That figure goes into the IRS worksheet that decides how much of her single benefit is taxed.
